titulo_es: Modals of deduction in the past
descripcion_es: Must have, might/may/could have, can't/couldn't have + past participle for making deductions about the past.
resumen: To deduce what probably happened we use modal + have + past participle: must have (surely yes), might/may/could have (perhaps), can't/couldn't have (surely not).

filas: The streets are wet. It must have rained.
might / may / could have + past participle
She might have missed the bus.
might not / may not have + past participle
He may not have received my email.
You can't have seen Juan; he's in Peru.

explicacion.texto: Spanish usually uses “debe de haber”, “habrá + participio” or “seguro que”: “Habrá perdido el tren” = He must have missed the train. “No ha podido verte” = He can't have seen you.
Careful: the opposite of must have is NOT mustn't have, but can't have / couldn't have. And couldn't have (it was impossible) is not the same as might not have (perhaps not).

items: Continuous form for actions in progress: She must have been sleeping when I called.
Could have also expresses an unrealised possibility: You could have been killed! (Spanish “podrías haberte matado”).
Should have + past participle is not deduction but criticism or expectation: You should have told me.

ejemplos.frase: The lights are off. They must have gone out.
ejemplos.traduccion: Las luces están apagadas. Habrán salido.

ejemplos.frase: I can't find my keys. I might have left them at the office.
ejemplos.traduccion: No encuentro las llaves. Puede que me las haya dejado en la oficina.

ejemplos.frase: She can't have written this report; she was on holiday all month.
ejemplos.traduccion: Ella no puede haber escrito este informe; estuvo de vacaciones todo el mes.

ejemplos.frase: He looks exhausted. He must have been working all night.
ejemplos.traduccion: Parece agotado. Debe de haber estado trabajando toda la noche.

ejemplos.frase: The parcel may not have arrived yet because of the strike.
ejemplos.traduccion: Puede que el paquete no haya llegado todavía por la huelga.

ejemplos.frase: Who could have sent me these flowers?

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: He mustn't have heard the phone.
errores_hispanohablantes.bien: He can't have heard the phone.
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: For a certain negative deduction you use can't/couldn't have.
After the modal always comes have (infinitive), never had.

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: They must lose the match yesterday.
errores_hispanohablantes.bien: They must have lost the match yesterday.
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: For a deduction about the past you need have + past participle.

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete with must have, might have or can't have + past participle.
ejercicios.frase: Laura's car isn't outside. She ___ (leave) already.
ejercicios.explicacion: The first row of the table applies: almost certainly yes = must have + past participle. The clue is the present evidence (her car isn't there), which leads to a firm conclusion about the past. The past participle of leave is left, so must have left (or the contraction must've left).
ejercicios.traduccion: El coche de Laura no está fuera. Ya se habrá ido.

errores_previstos.respuesta: must leave
errores_previstos.explicacion: Without have + past participle the deduction refers to the present or is an obligation; for the past you need must have left.

errores_previstos.respuesta: must have leaved
errores_previstos.explicacion: Leave is irregular: the past participle is left.

errores_previstos.respuesta: must had left
errores_previstos.explicacion: After a modal always comes have in the infinitive, never had.

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete with must have, might have or can't have + past participle.
ejercicios.frase: You ___ (see) Peter at the party. He was in hospital that night.
ejercicios.explicacion: The table's rule for almost certainly not is can't / couldn't have + past participle. The clue is the second sentence: he was in hospital, so it is impossible that he was at the party. The card stresses that the opposite of must have is can't have, not mustn't have; the full forms cannot and could not are accepted.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: It is impossible for a clear reason: can't/couldn't have.
ejercicios.traduccion: No puedes haber visto a Peter en la fiesta. Estaba en el hospital esa noche.

errores_previstos.respuesta: mustn't have seen
errores_previstos.explicacion: Mustn't have is not used for deduction: the certain negative deduction is can't have.

errores_previstos.respuesta: might not have seen
errores_previstos.explicacion: Might not have only expresses a possibility; here there is evidence that makes it impossible: can't have.

errores_previstos.respuesta: can't have saw
errores_previstos.explicacion: After have comes the past participle (seen), not the past simple (saw).

ejercicios.frase: The phone was busy for an hour. She ___ (talk) to her mother.
ejercicios.explicacion: The card's list explains the continuous form for actions in progress: modal + have been + -ing. The clue is was busy for an hour: the action lasted for some time. Must have been talking expresses near certainty; might, may or could have been talking express possibility, and all of them are accepted because the instruction only asks for the continuous form.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Action in progress in the past: modal + have been + -ing.
ejercicios.traduccion: El teléfono estuvo comunicando una hora. Debía de estar hablando con su madre.

errores_previstos.respuesta: must have talked
errores_previstos.explicacion: It is correct as a deduction, but the instruction asks for the continuous form, which stresses the duration: must have been talking.

errores_previstos.respuesta: must be talking
errores_previstos.explicacion: Must be talking refers to the present; the action is past and requires have been.

errores_previstos.respuesta: must have been talk
errores_previstos.explicacion: After have been comes the verb in -ing: talking.

ejercicios.frase: I'm not sure why he's late. He ___ have got lost.
ejercicios.explicacion: The second row of the table, possible, uses might / may / could have + past participle. The clue is I'm not sure: there is no certainty, only a hypothesis. That is why all three forms are fine: might, may or could have got lost.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: We are not sure: might/may/could have.
ejercicios.traduccion: No estoy seguro de por qué llega tarde. Puede que se haya perdido.

errores_previstos.respuesta: must
errores_previstos.explicacion: Must indicates near certainty, and the sentence says I'm not sure.

errores_previstos.respuesta: can
errores_previstos.explicacion: Can have is not used for possibility in affirmative sentences; you say might, may or could have.

ejercicios.frase: The window is broken and the TV has gone. Someone ___ into the house.
ejercicios.explicacion: The rule of must have + past participle for almost certain deductions applies. The evidence (broken window, missing TV) leads to a firm conclusion about something that has already happened. Break into means to enter a place to steal, and its past participle is broken.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: The evidence leads to an almost certain conclusion.
ejercicios.traduccion: La ventana está rota y la tele ha desaparecido. Alguien ha debido de entrar en la casa.

por_opcion.must have broken: Correct: almost certain deduction about the past.
por_opcion.can't have broken: Incorrect: it would say that it is impossible, the opposite of what the evidence shows.
por_opcion.should have broken: Incorrect: should have expresses criticism or an unfulfilled expectation, not deduction.
por_opcion.must break: Incorrect: without have + past participle it does not refer to the past; it would sound like an obligation.

ejercicios.frase: He ___ the exam; he never studies and yet he got an A! Maybe he cheated.
ejercicios.explicacion: The table gives can't have + past participle for almost certainly not. The clue is he never studies: we know he does not study, so it is impossible that he prepared, which is why we suspect that he cheated (maybe he cheated).
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: We know he never studies: it is impossible that he prepared.
ejercicios.traduccion: No puede haberse preparado el examen; nunca estudia ¡y aun así ha sacado un sobresaliente! Quizá copió.

por_opcion.can't have prepared for: Correct: impossibility deduced from what we know about him.
por_opcion.must have prepared for: Incorrect: it contradicts he never studies and the suspicion that he cheated.
por_opcion.should have prepared for: Incorrect: should have is a criticism (he ought to have prepared), not a deduction; it does not explain the “maybe he cheated”.

ejercicios.frase: I don't know where Ana is. She ___ to the gym, but I'm not sure.
ejercicios.explicacion: The row for possible applies: may / might / could have + past participle. The clue is I don't know and I'm not sure: there is only a hypothesis. May have gone is the only option that expresses possibility without certainty.
ejercicios.traduccion: No sé dónde está Ana. Puede que haya ido al gimnasio, pero no estoy seguro.

por_opcion.must have gone: Incorrect: it indicates near certainty, incompatible with I'm not sure.
por_opcion.can't have gone: Incorrect: it denies the possibility, whereas the sentence is suggesting it.

ejercicios.frase: They mustn't have received the invitation, because they didn't reply.
respuestas: They can't have received the invitation, because they didn't reply.
They couldn't have received the invitation, because they didn't reply.
They might not have received the invitation, because they didn't reply.
They may not have received the invitation, because they didn't reply.
ejercicios.explicacion: The card explains that mustn't have is not used for deduction: the certain negative deduction is can't have or couldn't have. If the speaker only wants to suggest it as a possibility, might not have or may not have are fine. That is why all four forms are accepted.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Mustn't have is not used for deduction; use can't/couldn't have (or might not have if it is a possibility).
ejercicios.traduccion: No pueden haber recibido la invitación, porque no han contestado.

errores_previstos.respuesta: They mustn't have received the invitation, because they didn't reply.
errores_previstos.explicacion: This is the uncorrected sentence: mustn't have does not express deduction.

errores_previstos.respuesta: They mustn't receive the invitation, because they didn't reply.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Mustn't receive is a prohibition in the present; to make a deduction about the past you need can't have received.

errores_previstos.respuesta: They can't have receive the invitation, because they didn't reply.
errores_previstos.explicacion: After have comes the past participle: received.

ejercicios.frase: She must has forgotten our appointment.
respuestas: She must have forgotten our appointment.
ejercicios.explicacion: The card's second typical error: after the modal always comes have in the infinitive, never has or had, even if the subject is she. Modals are not conjugated, and the verb that follows them is in the base form. The contraction must've is also accepted.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: After a modal comes have, not has.
ejercicios.traduccion: Ha debido de olvidarse de nuestra cita.

errores_previstos.respuesta: She must has forgotten our appointment.
errores_previstos.explicacion: This is the uncorrected sentence: after must comes have, not has.

errores_previstos.respuesta: She must had forgotten our appointment.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Not had either: after a modal, have in the base form.

errores_previstos.respuesta: She must have forgot our appointment.
errores_previstos.explicacion: The past participle of forget is forgotten; forgot is the past simple.

ejercicios.frase: The road is wet; it must rain during the night.
respuestas: The road is wet; it must have rained during the night.
ejercicios.explicacion: The card's general rule applies: for a deduction about the past you need have + past participle. The clue is during the night (past) as opposed to the present evidence (the road is wet). Must rain without have would refer to the present or to an obligation.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Deduction about the past: must have + past participle.
ejercicios.traduccion: La carretera está mojada; ha debido de llover durante la noche.

errores_previstos.respuesta: The road is wet; it must rain during the night.
errores_previstos.explicacion: This is the uncorrected sentence: have + past participle is missing for the past.

errores_previstos.respuesta: The road is wet; it must rained during the night.
errores_previstos.explicacion: A modal cannot be followed by a past simple; you need have rained.

errores_previstos.respuesta: The road is wet; it must have rain during the night.
errores_previstos.explicacion: After have comes the past participle: rained.

ejercicios.enunciado: Rewrite the sentence with must have.
ejercicios.frase: I'm sure Tom forgot about the meeting.
respuestas: Tom must have forgotten about the meeting.
Tom must've forgotten about the meeting.
ejercicios.explicacion: The card equates I'm sure + past with must have + past participle. The subject becomes Tom, and forgot (past simple) becomes have forgotten (past participle). About the meeting stays the same.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: I'm sure + past = must have + past participle.
ejercicios.traduccion: Tom ha debido de olvidarse de la reunión.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Tom must forget about the meeting.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Without have + past participle it does not refer to the past; it would sound like an obligation.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Tom must have forgot about the meeting.
errores_previstos.explicacion: The past participle of forget is forgotten.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Tom must had forgotten about the meeting.
errores_previstos.explicacion: After must comes have, never had.

ejercicios.enunciado: Rewrite the sentence with can't have.
ejercicios.frase: It's impossible that they finished the job so quickly.
respuestas: They can't have finished the job so quickly.
They cannot have finished the job so quickly.
ejercicios.explicacion: The card establishes that It's impossible that + past is equivalent to can't have + past participle. Finished is already a regular past participle, so the result is can't have finished. Cannot have finished, the full form, is also accepted.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: It's impossible that + past = can't have + past participle.
ejercicios.traduccion: No pueden haber terminado el trabajo tan deprisa.

errores_previstos.respuesta: They mustn't have finished the job so quickly.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Mustn't have does not express impossibility; you use can't have.

errores_previstos.respuesta: They can't finish the job so quickly.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Without have + past participle the sentence talks about the present or about ability, not about a past fact.

errores_previstos.respuesta: They couldn't finish the job so quickly.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Couldn't finish means that they were not able to; the deduction of impossibility requires have: can't have finished.

ejercicios.enunciado: Rewrite the sentence with might have.
ejercicios.frase: Perhaps she took the wrong train.
respuestas: She might have taken the wrong train.
She might've taken the wrong train.
ejercicios.explicacion: The card equates perhaps + past with might have + past participle. Took, the past simple of take, becomes the past participle: taken. Perhaps disappears because might already expresses the possibility, and the rest of the sentence (the wrong train) stays unchanged.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Perhaps + past = might have + past participle.
ejercicios.traduccion: Puede que haya cogido el tren equivocado.

errores_previstos.respuesta: She might have took the wrong train.
errores_previstos.explicacion: After have comes the past participle taken, not the past simple took.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Perhaps she might have taken the wrong train.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Perhaps and might express the same thing; keeping both is redundant and the transformation asks you to replace it.

errores_previstos.respuesta: She might take the wrong train.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Without have + past participle it refers to the future or the present, not to the past.

ejercicios.explicacion: The structure is subject + must have + past participle, for an almost certain deduction about the past. Overslept is the past participle of oversleep (to sleep too long and not wake up on time). Must always goes before have.

errores_previstos.respuesta: he have must overslept
errores_previstos.explicacion: The modal goes first and then have: must have.

errores_previstos.respuesta: must he have overslept
errores_previstos.explicacion: That order forms a question; a statement is required.

ejercicios.explicacion: This is the continuous form on the card: must have been + -ing, for an action in progress in the past. The fixed order is subject, must, have, been and the verb in -ing. Joking means not being serious.

errores_previstos.respuesta: they must been have joking
errores_previstos.explicacion: The order is must have been, never been have.

errores_previstos.respuesta: they have must been joking
errores_previstos.explicacion: The modal goes before have.

descripcion_larga_es: Past modals of deduction (must have, might/may/could have, can't/couldn't have + past participle) are used to draw conclusions from evidence about what probably happened. They matter because Spanish expresses this with “habrá + participio” or “debe de haber”, without an exact parallel, and because Spanish speakers often use mustn't have where English requires can't have.

contexto.que_es: It is the combination of a modal with have + past participle to express the degree of certainty about a past fact: almost certainly yes (must have), possible (might, may, could have), possibly not (might not, may not have) and almost certainly not (can't, couldn't have).
contexto.por_que_importa: It allows you to reason aloud about causes and explanations, something frequent when commenting on news, data or situations. Using the wrong modal changes the degree of certainty: mustn't have is not understood as a deduction, and might not have is not equivalent to couldn't have. In B2 exams it is a classic point in transformations.
contexto.cuando_se_usa: When there is present evidence about something past (the ground is wet, it has rained) or when rephrasing I'm sure, perhaps or it's impossible that + past. Spanish usually uses the future perfect of conjecture (“habrá salido”), which Spanish speakers do not know how to carry over, and they tend to say must lose instead of must have lost.
